Spontaneous continuous motor unit single discharges
Andreas Posa MD 1 | Izabela Ni /C19skiewicz MD1 | Valerian Raescu MD 1 |
Alexander Emmer MD 1 | Alexey Surov MD 2 | Malte Kornhuber MD 1,3
1Department of Neurology, University
Hospital of Halle, Halle (Saale), Germany
2Department of Diagnostic and Interventional
Radiology, University Hospital of Leipzig,
Leipzig, Germany
3Department of Neurology, Helios Hospital
Sangerhausen, Sangerhausen, Germany
Correspondence
Andreas Posa, Martin-Luther-University Halle-
Wittenberg, Department of Neurology, Ernst-
Grube-Straße 40, 06120 Halle (Saale),
Germany.
Email: andreas.posa@medizin.uni-halle.de
Abstract
Introduction: Motor unit hyperexcitability (MUH) may become manifest in needle
electromyography (EMG) recordings as fasciculation potentials, myokymic discharges,
or neuromyotonic discharges. Here, we describe a further MUH phenomenon.
Methods: Needle EMG recordings of the Neurology Hospital of Halle (Saale) stored
in a video mode as .wav data between 2000 and 2015 were screened for spontane-
ous continuous motor unit single discharges (SCMUSD).
Results: We identified 23 video needle EMG waveforms from 14 patients with
SCMUSD. The corresponding motor units discharged at a rate of about 6 H Z (6.3
± 4.0; range, 1.3-18.1). The coefficient of variation of the discharge rate was 3.5%
± 1.7%. Neurogenic disorders were diagnosed in 12 patients, limb girdle muscle
dystrophy was diagnosed in one patient, and stiff-limb syndrome was diagnosed in
one patient.
Discussion: Spontaneous continuous motor unit single discharge, as described here,
widens the spectrum of MUH phenomena.
KEYWORDS
axonal sprouting, jitter, motor unit hyperexcitability, needle electromyography,
neuromyotonia, spontaneous activity
1 | INTRODUCTION
Motor unit hyperexciteability (MUH) may become manifest by a
wide variety of phenomena that can be recorded by needle elec-
tromyography (EMG). Well known examples are fasciculation
potentials, myokymic discharges, and neuromyotonic high fre-
quency discharges. Motor unit hyperexciteability has been reported
to occur in central nervous system diseases such as stiff person
syndrome,
1 syringomyelia, 2 and poststroke spasticity. 3 Generalized
MUH may be observed in amyotrophic lateral sclerosis 4 or result
from autoantibody blockade of axonal ion channels, as in Isaac syn-
drome.1 Focal MUH has been reported in different disorders of the
peripheral nervous system, 5,6 such as compression radiculopathy,
plexus lesions, focal peripheral nerve lesions, and polyneuropathies.
Here, we describe a form of MUH with continuous MU single
discharges.
2 | MATERIALS AND METHODS
Among 10 437 video EMG recordings from the clinical electrophysiol-
ogy department of the Neurological Clinic of the University Hospital
Halle (Saale) from January 1, 2001 to July 12, 2015, 1411 recordings
were analyzed for the existence of spontaneous continuous motor unit
single discharges (SCMUSD) in video files that had been obtained when
an unusual pathological finding was noticed during a diagnostic EMG
examination with 26 gauge concentric needle electrodes (CareFusion)
with Toennies Multiliner or Toennies NeuroScreen XP. Filter setting
were 5 H Z to 5 kHZ. In the files, the sample rate was 10 kHZ.
The following data were searched: age, sex, diagnosis, recorded
muscle, motor unit (MU) discharge rate (H Z), coefficient of variation of
MU discharges (from 50 subsequent SCMUSD), and MU potential

amplitude and duration. For coefficient of variation calculations, the
intervals between the most stable and prominent peak component
were measured. A crude estimation was made for the presence of jitter
or blocking, which was not the main focus of this study. To do so, sub-
sequent MU potentials were displayed as a cascade, and jitter and
blocking were judged by visual inspection. The study was approved by
the ethics committee of the Martin Luther University Halle-Wittenberg.

MU, motor unit; MUH, motor unit hyperexcitability; MUP, motor unit potential;
SCMUSD, spontaneous continuous motor unit single discharge.

3 | RESULTS
Spontaneous continuous motor unit single discharges were identified
in 24 recordings from 14 patients. Clinical and EMG data are pres-
ented in Table 1. The patients were 61.1 ± 15.1 years old (range,
32-81), and seven were women. Except for one patient with stiff
limb syndrome and one patient with a calpainopathy type of muscle
dystrophy, neurogenic processes were diagnosed in all patients,
namely motor neuron disease (three) or different types of peripheral
nerve disorders (nine). Spontaneous continuous motor unit single
discharges (Videos S1, S2, and S3) were present in various muscles
and were usually identified in only one or two instances per patient.
However, in the patient with HINT1 (histidine triad nucleotide bind-
ing protein 1) polyneuropathy, seven different SCMUSDs were
recorded in two different muscles. The involved MU potentials dis-
charged continuously without silent intervals at a rate of about
6 H Z (6.3 ± 4.0; range, 1.3-18.1). The coefficient of variation was
3.5% ± 1.7%. Stiff limb syndrome (18.1 H Z), amyotrophic lateral
sclerosis (15.5 H Z), or chronic inflammatory demyelinating poly-
neuropathy (11.7 H Z) were diagnosed in patients with relatively
high MU discharge rates. Kennedy syndrome (1.3 H Z), calpainopathy
type of muscle dystrophy (1.7 H Z), or polyneuropathy due to
Sjögren syndrome (3.1 H Z) were diagnosed in patients with espe-
cially low MU discharge rates. There was a significant positive corre-
lation between coefficient of variation and MU discharge frequency
(Figure 1; P < .01; Kendall's τ). Motor unit potential amplitudes were
in the normal range or lower (0.29 ± 0.22 mV). Motor unit potential
duration was usually longer than normal (20.3 ± 12.7 ms). Blocking
within the MUP components was present in eight instances, and
jitter was increased in 12. When an increased jitter was detected,
MUP duration was significantly longer than in those instances with
apparently normal jitter (Figure 2; P < .005, Mann –Whitney U test).
No such difference in MUP duration was noted whether blocking
was present or absent, presumably due to the low number of MUPs
displaying blocking.

4 | DISCUSSION
In contrast to myokymic discharges, which consist of bursts of 2, 3, or
more MUPs from the same MU, SCMUSDs are confined to single MUP
that repeat at relatively constant intervals. Spontaneous continuous
motor unit single discharges have not been observed in patients with
disorders that have finally been diagnosed to be functional in nature.
Therefore, SCMUSD can likely be taken as an abnormal phenomenon.
In our case series, the majority of the diagnoses were neurogenic pro-
cesses. In one patient, a calpainopathy type of muscular dystrophy had
been diagnosed. In calpainopathy, a broad spectrum of symptoms may
be present, and neurogenic phenomena in EMG recordings are not
uncommon.
7 In another patient, stiff limb syndrome was diagnosed.
Other motor hyperexcitability phenomena such as myokymic dis-
charges have been described previously in stiff person syndrome.
1
When the MUPs that were recorded as SCMUSDs were analyzed, the
majority could readily be identified as reinnervation potentials because
of their long durations and the temporal dispersion of the potential
components. The MUPs with a normal duration still could display signs
of impaired neuromuscular transmission such as blocking or an increase
in jitter relative to the potential component that was taken for trigger-
ing. Only excessively increased jitter could be identified reliably. Such
jitter was more often present in MUPs with a pathologically long dura-
tion than in MUPs with a normal duration (Figure 2). Thus, both an
increase in jitter and the presence of MUPs with an increased duration
can be taken as further hints that axonal sprouting may play a crucial
role in SCMUSD generation, at least in peripheral neurogenic processes.
The expression of ion channels has been shown to be altered in growth
cones of sprouting peripheral nerve axons.
8 Such alterations in ion
channel expression may be important in generating motor axonal spon-
taneous activity. The SCMUSD frequency of about 6 H Z presumably
corresponds to the specific depolarization characteristics of the
involved ion channels. In contrast to pathological muscle fiber sponta-
neous activity such as positive sharp waves or fibrillation potentials that
are characterized by constancy in repetition rate, SCMUSD repetition is
characterized by a somewhat less constant discharge rate with a coeffi-
cient of variation of 3.5% ± 1.7%. Whether this slight inconstancy in
SCMUSD generation is due to differences in depolarizing membrane
currents through membrane ion channels, inconstancies of action
potential propagation, differences in the amounts of transmitter quanta
released into the synaptic cleft remains to be established. A discharge
rate of 5.2 ± 1.6 H Z (coefficient of variation 5.4% ± 1.6%), which is
close to that reported here, has been detected in leg muscles after
long-lasting spinal cord injury. Thus, the similarity of the SCMUSD find-
ings in neurogenic processes and in the patient with stiff limb syndrome
may be due to similarities between axonal sprouts and in ventral horn
cells deafferented from upper motor neuron input. The coefficient of
variation observed in our investigation is definitively smaller than what
has been shown for voluntarily recruited MUs, which are in the range
of 9% to 47%.
9 This difference in coefficient of variation may facilitate
the distinction from voluntarily recruited MUs that might contaminate
recordings from incompletely relaxed patients.

In conclusion, SCMUSDs add to the spectrum of MUH phenom-
ena with continuous MU activity. Spontaneous continuous motor unit
single discharges appear to occur in a spectrum of diseases similar to
those associated with myokymic discharges.

Examination of the human motor endplate after brachial plexus
injury with two-photon microscopy

Abstract
Introduction: After traumatic nerve injury, neuromuscular junction remodeling plays
a key role in determining functional outcomes. Immunohistochemical analyses of
denervated muscle biopsies may provide valuable prognostic data regarding clinical
outcomes to supplement electrodiagnostic studies.
Methods: We performed biopsies on nonfunctioning deltoid muscles in two patients
after gunshot wounds and visualized the neuromuscular junctions using two-photon
microscopy with immunohistochemistry.
Results: Although the nerves in both patients showed evidence of acute Wallerian
degeneration, some of the motor endplates were intact but exhibited significantly
decreased surface area and volume. Both patients exhibited substantial recovery of
motor function over several weeks postinjury.
Discussion: Two-photon microscopic assessment of neuromuscular junction integrity
and motor endplate morphometry in muscle biopsies provided evidence of partial
sparing of muscle innervation. This finding supported the clinical judgment that even-
tual recovery would occur. With further study, this technique may help to guide
operative decisionmaking after traumatic nerve injuries.
KEYWORDS
brachial plexus injury, gunshot wound, motor endplate, neuromuscular junction, traumatic
nerve injury
1 | INTRODUCTION
After brachial plexus injuries (BPIs), some patients have spontane-
ous recovery, whereas others req uire surgical intervention to
improve their functional outcome. 1,2 Formulating diagnostic
criteria to identify patients who may benefit from surgery is a
high priority. Magnetic resonance imaging and ultrasound are
both useful for identifying damaged nerves preoperatively, but
they cannot predict reg eneration potential,
3-5 which depends on
the viability of the motor endplate (MEP) within targeted muscle
fibers. 6
